topics.title: What am I doing wrong?
topics.text:
Hi guys. I was looking at this problem and I am confused why my answer is wrong.

This is the Problem:



Seven different prizes are to be distributed among three contest winners such

that each winner receives at least one prize and each of the prizes goes to one

of the three winners. In how many different ways can the prizes be distributed

among the three winners?



Here is my method:

SolutionSince everyone needs to have at least one prize we try to work with this first:

$\binom{7}{3}\cdot3!$ which is $210$.

Now we have 4 presents to give and the three winners. Using sticks and stones (what I call it) there are

$\binom{6}{2}=15$ ways to distribute them

Therefore my answer is $210 \times 15=\boxed{3150.}$



Where did I go wrong?

Help is much appreciated

topics.title: Probability and Algebra Meet
topics.text: 13. Two adjacent jars each have 90 balls. Each jar has b black balls, w white balls and r red  balls. A ball is drawn at random from each jar. Let x be the probability that both are black, y  be the probability that both are white and z be the probability that both are red. If z=x+y how many marbles are there of each color?

topics.title: Ant on a Hypercube
topics.text: An ant goes on a random walk on a unit hypercube.  It starts at a vertex of the hypercube, and walks on its edges.  Whenever there is another vertex, the ant goes down a random edge- including the one it just walked on.  If the ant's trip ends when it meets its starting point once more, what is the expected length of the ant's trip in units?

topics.title: k Rubix Cube Problem.
topics.text:
I define an orientation of a rubix cube to be a rearrangement of the pieces such that it's form appears the same as a regular rubix cube, and the stickers on respective pieces have not been rearranged. If one orientation can be transformed to another by twisting the cube, they are considered the same.



How many distinct orientations of a rubix cube are there?



clarificationIf a cube is solvable, it is the same as the solved state of the rubix cube
